prompt.context: Marble Front Supplies is a producer of kitchen appliances and kitchen supplies. Marble Front is a strong brand, and historically the company had significant advertising and marketing expenses to maintain their brand. In the past, growth has been steady, driven by a combination of product line extensions and key acquisitions of specialty item producers. Sales go through a number of channels, including superstores, which are increasingly critical. These superstores have gained considerable share in the past few years, and constantly pressure us to lower our margins as they substitute generic products for traditional brand names like Marble Front. Recent drops in sales and profits have made Marble Front an acquisition target.
prompt.question: Our client is a private equity firm considering purchasing Marble Front. The client wants us to do due diligence on Marble Front's production facilities, and wants us to size the opportunity for production efficiencies. They believe Marble Front needs to lower costs to stay competitive in this market. What are the factors we should examine to determine whether Marble Front can lower production costs?

clarifying_info.a: Current production generates $475 million in revenues.

clarifying_info.q: How many factories does the client operate and where?
clarifying_info.a: The client currently produces SKUs (Stock Keeping Units) in 3 factories located in Michigan, Mexico, and New Jersey.

clarifying_info.q: Can you share production and capacity data?
clarifying_info.a: Michigan: 5,000 SKUs produced, 8,500 SKU capacity. Mexico: 4,500 SKUs produced, 12,000 SKU capacity. New Jersey: 3,000 SKUs produced, 5,500 SKU capacity. (See Exhibit #1)
See Exhibit #2 for fixed annual costs and variable annual operating costs per SKU by facility.

exhibits.title: Annual Production vs. Annual Capacity by Factory
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing annual production (used) versus annual capacity for each of three factories: Michigan, Mexico, and New Jersey.

exhibits.title: Fixed Annual Costs and Variable Annual Operating Costs by Factory
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts side by side: (1) Fixed Annual Costs in $MM per factory, and (2) Variable Annual Operating Costs per SKU per factory, for Michigan, Mexico, and New Jersey.

framework: Capacity utilization: assess current production vs. capacity across all three plants
Cost structure: break down fixed vs. variable costs by plant to identify cost drivers
Consolidation scenarios: evaluate options for combining plants to reduce total cost
Revenue impact: assess any revenue loss from production reduction in consolidation
Implementation costs and risks: closing costs, union contracts, capital leases, hiring costs for expansion
Strategic considerations: flexibility for future demand growth, public perception of offshoring

questions.prompt: What is the current capacity utilization across all three plants?
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum production across all plants (12,500 SKUs) and total capacity (26,000 SKUs) and divide to get ~48%. Key insight: the company is running at roughly half capacity overall, suggesting significant room for consolidation.

math.setup: Total production = Michigan + Mexico + New Jersey production. Total capacity = Michigan + Mexico + New Jersey capacity. Utilization = Total production / Total capacity.

questions.prompt: What is the current total annual cost of running all three plants? What conclusions can you draw about fixed and variable costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total cost for each plant (fixed + production × variable cost per SKU) and sum them. Michigan is high-variable-cost; Mexico is the lowest variable cost but has highest capacity; New Jersey has the highest variable cost and highest fixed cost per SKU produced. Mexico is the most cost-efficient plant.

math.setup: Total cost per plant = Fixed annual cost + (Annual production × Variable cost per SKU). Then sum all three.

questions.prompt: How much would we save under Scenario #1: combining New Jersey into Michigan?
questions.guidance: Savings = fixed costs eliminated (NJ fixed costs) + variable cost savings on NJ production moved to Michigan (NJ variable cost minus Michigan variable cost, multiplied by NJ production). Michigan has sufficient remaining capacity (8,500 - 5,000 = 3,500 spare) to absorb NJ's 3,000 SKUs.

math.setup: Savings = NJ fixed costs + (NJ variable cost per SKU - Michigan variable cost per SKU) × NJ production

questions.prompt: How much would we save under Scenario #2a: combining Michigan into Mexico?
questions.guidance: Savings = Michigan fixed costs eliminated + variable cost savings on Michigan production moved to Mexico. Mexico has capacity: 12,000 - 4,500 = 7,500 spare, enough for Michigan's 5,000 SKUs.

math.setup: Savings = Michigan fixed costs + (Michigan variable cost per SKU - Mexico variable cost per SKU) × Michigan production

questions.prompt: How much would we save under Scenario #2b: combining New Jersey into Mexico?
questions.guidance: Savings = NJ fixed costs + variable cost savings on NJ production moved to Mexico. Mexico has sufficient capacity to absorb NJ's 3,000 SKUs.

math.setup: Savings = NJ fixed costs + (NJ variable cost per SKU - Mexico variable cost per SKU) × NJ production

questions.prompt: How much would we save under Scenario #3: combining both Michigan and New Jersey into Mexico, reducing total SKUs from 12,500 to Mexico's capacity of 12,000?
questions.guidance: Mexico's capacity is 12,000 SKUs, so consolidating all production there requires a 500 SKU reduction (4% of current production), causing a revenue loss. Net savings = cost savings minus revenue loss. Candidate should recognize this tradeoff.

math.setup: New total cost = Mexico fixed + (Mexico capacity × Mexico variable cost per SKU). Cost savings = $136M - new cost. Revenue loss = (production decrease / original production) × total revenues. Net savings = cost savings - revenue loss.

questions.prompt: What other costs or revenues should we consider when sizing the consolidation opportunity? How high would closing costs have to be before Scenario #3 is no longer the best option?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates raise implementation/transition costs and strategic risks. On the threshold question: if per-plant closing costs exceed ~$16.5M, Scenario #2a becomes more profitable than Scenario #3. Separately, if NJ closing costs exceed ~$14.5M, combining only Michigan into Mexico (Scenario #2a) is preferable to Scenario #3.

math.setup: Compare marginal benefit of Scenario #3 over Scenario #2a against the additional plant closing cost.
steps: Scenario #3 saves ~$49M; Scenario #2a saves $34.5M; marginal benefit of closing NJ as well: ~$14.5–16.5M
If per-plant closing cost > ~$16.5M, Scenario #2a dominates Scenario #3

brainstorming.prompt: What other costs or revenues might we consider when sizing the opportunity of production consolidation?

categories.name: Implementation and transition costs
ideas: Hiring and training costs for expanding Mexico plant

categories.name: Strategic and operational risks
ideas: Loss of production flexibility — Mexico at full capacity leaves no room for demand growth
Supply chain disruption risk during transition
Quality control risks when scaling up a single facility
Geopolitical or currency risk concentrated in Mexico

categories.name: External and reputational factors
ideas: Public backlash from outsourcing manufacturing jobs to Mexico
Brand risk from perception of offshoring
Regulatory or tariff changes affecting Mexico operations

categories.name: Revenue considerations
ideas: Revenue loss from reduced SKU count in Scenario #3
Potential pricing pressure if quality is perceived to change
Opportunity to reinvest savings into marketing to offset superstore pricing pressure

recommendation: Recommend Scenario #3: consolidate all production into Mexico at full capacity (12,000 SKUs), generating net annual savings of approximately $49M — the highest of all scenarios
This requires accepting a modest ~4% ($19M) revenue reduction from dropping 500 SKUs, but delivers substantially higher cost savings than any alternative
risks: Mexico at full capacity eliminates flexibility for unexpected demand growth or new product launches
Per-plant closing costs above ~$14.5–16.5M erode Scenario #3's advantage over Scenario #2a
Public and political backlash from closing US plants and moving all production to Mexico
Concentration risk: single-site production creates operational vulnerability
next_steps: Obtain detailed estimates for plant closing costs (union buyouts, lease terminations, severance) to confirm Scenario #3 remains optimal
Model capacity expansion options at Mexico facility to preserve some upside flexibility
Develop a phased transition plan to minimize revenue disruption during consolidation
Assess Mexico operational risks including currency exposure, labor market, and regulatory environment
